author: Mark
title: Alex Soros Can't Stop Gloating About Democrats Big Win
text:
Within hours of the 2026 midterm results rolling in, Alex Soros — son of billionaire megadonor George Soros — posted a celebration so breathless it read like a man who'd just watched his investment portfolio double overnight. "In one night, America changed for generations to come," he wrote. "The greatest victory I have ever seen!"
Not "our" victory. Not "the people's" victory. His.
The full statement went further: "The world changed yesterday. This wasn't just a midterm or a blue wave. It was something this country has never seen before." The younger Soros wasn't just pleased. He was savoring. A man whose family has spent billions bankrolling left-wing causes across the globe wanted everyone to know this one felt personal.
Midterm losses for the party in power aren't unusual. Bill Clinton lost 54 House seats in 1994. Barack Obama lost 63 House seats in 2010 and 9 Senate seats in 2014. The pattern is as old as modern politics. What's new is the donor class skipping the usual practiced humility and running a public victory lap before the votes are even fully counted.
Alex Soros isn't an elected official. He didn't campaign. He didn't knock on doors or debate an opponent under stage lights. He wrote checks. And now he's posting like he personally flipped every swing district in the country.
The reaction online was pointed. One commenter noted, "That didn't happen.. you have majorities but no mandate." Another pointed out that Trump took his 2024 win as a mandate and governed accordingly — something Democrats spent two years calling authoritarian. Now their biggest financier is claiming a mandate of his own on election night, and the same crowd finds it inspiring.
What makes the gloating particularly revealing is what Alex Soros chose not to say. He didn't credit any candidate. He didn't name a single policy victory. He didn't mention a district or a state or a ballot measure. The celebration was entirely about the raw result — seats flipped, power shifted, the scoreboard updated. This wasn't about governance. It was about the game.
George Soros built a political empire by staying just far enough behind the curtain to maintain plausible deniability. The elder Soros funded district attorney races, media ventures, and voter registration drives for decades while his defenders dismissed any mention of his influence as conspiracy theory. The son has apparently decided the curtain is no longer necessary.
That's the shift worth watching. The Soros political operation used to operate with at least a veneer of institutional distance — foundations, nonprofits, intermediaries with anodyne names. Alex Soros posting "the greatest victory I have ever seen" on the morning after an election is the donor class telling you, to your face, that they consider this their win.
Clinton lost 54 seats and blamed his own overreach. Obama lost 63 and called it a "shellacking." Alex Soros watched the other side of that equation and called it the greatest thing he's ever witnessed.
He didn't even wait for the final tallies.
